items.prompt: In the lunchbox picture, which Docker word is the sealed lunchbox itself?
choices: Image
Container
Registry
items.explanation: The image is the packed, sealed artifact. Nothing is running yet.

items.prompt: Which Docker word means the lunchbox is open and being eaten from?
choices: Image
Dockerfile
Container
items.explanation: A container is an image that has been started as a running instance.

items.prompt: What is the Dockerfile in the lunchbox picture?
choices: The lunchbox once it is sealed and ready
The desk where it gets opened
The recipe for packing the lunchbox
items.explanation: The Dockerfile holds the instructions. Building it produces the image.

items.prompt: You start the same image three times. What do you get?
choices: One container shared three ways
Three separate containers
Three images with new names
items.explanation: Each start is its own container. The image stays one fixed artifact.

items.prompt: Can an image change while containers from it are running?
choices: Yes, each container edits it as it runs
No, an image is read-only and fixed
Yes, but only the newest container may
items.explanation: Containers write to their own top layer, never to the image beneath.

items.prompt: Which pairing is closest to a class and an object?
choices: Image and container
Container and image
Registry and Dockerfile
items.explanation: One definition (the image) can produce many live instances (containers).

items.prompt: What happens to a container's temporary files when it is removed?
choices: They disappear with the container
They are added to the image
They are copied into the registry
items.explanation: The writable layer belongs to the container, so removing it removes the files.

items.prompt: Which command builds an image from a Dockerfile?
choices: docker run
docker restart
docker build
items.explanation: build makes the image, run starts a container from it, push uploads it.

items.prompt: A teammate edits a config file inside a running container, then removes that container and starts a new one from the same image. Is the edit still there?
choices: No, the edit sat in the removed container's own layer, so a new container starts from the untouched image
Yes, because the edit was saved into the image as soon as that container stopped being used by anyone
Yes, because Docker copies a container's writable layer into the registry when that container is removed
No, because an image is deleted from the host whenever one of its containers is removed
items.explanation: The edit went into the old container's top layer, which is discarded with the container. The image was never touched.
items.reference:
The lunchbox picture
Dockerfile: the recipe for packing the lunchbox
image: the sealed lunchbox, packed once and never changed
container: one lunchbox opened and in use at a desk
many desks, one packed lunchbox design: many containers, one image
Why: an image is a fixed package; a container is a running instance of it with its own throwaway writable layer.
items.learnMore:
Image and container

Building happens once per version and produces the image. Running can happen any number of times, on any machine that has the image, and each run is a separate container. Whatever a container writes while running lives in its own top layer and goes away with it.

Common mistake

Treating a container as a place to save changes. Edits made inside a running container are not in the image; to change what future containers start with, change the Dockerfile and build a new image.
items.reflection: Think of something you prepare once and use many times, such as a template or a checklist. What plays the role of the image, and what plays the container?

items.prompt: CI builds image X once. Staging and production both start containers from X. What does this guarantee?
choices: Both hold identical data, since the image carries the database contents that each environment reads from it
Both run the same packaged files and runtime, so differences come from config or data outside the image
Both behave the same under load, because the image also fixes the CPU and memory each one gets at run time
Both start instantly, because images are loaded into memory when built rather than when they run
items.explanation: An image fixes what is packaged: code, runtime, libraries. Settings, data and resource limits are supplied at run time, so they can still differ.

An image is written by hand into a Dockerfile, and the Dockerfile is then started as a container
A container is built once from a Dockerfile, and images are the copies it makes while it runs
A Dockerfile is built into an image once, and the image starts as many containers as needed

items.prompt: Two containers start from the same image. One writes a file to /tmp/note. Can the other see it?
choices: No, each container gets its own writable layer on top of the shared read-only image layers
Yes, because both containers share one filesystem copy that any of them is allowed to write to
Yes, but only after the image is rebuilt so that the new file is included in its layers
No, but only because the second container was started a while after the first one
items.explanation: The image layers are shared and read-only. Writes go to a per-container layer, so siblings cannot see each other's changes.

items.prompt: What does a virtual machine carry that a container does not?
choices: A faster way to share files between hosts
A smaller image than any container
Its own whole guest operating system
items.explanation: Each VM boots a full guest OS. Containers skip that.

items.prompt: What do all containers on one machine share?
choices: One writable layer
The host's kernel
A single running process
items.explanation: The kernel is the shared table. Everything else is per-container.

items.prompt: Which one usually starts faster?
choices: A virtual machine
A container
They always take equal time
items.explanation: A container just starts a process. A VM boots an operating system first.

items.prompt: Which gives the stronger wall between neighbours?
choices: A virtual machine
A container
Both walls are identical
items.explanation: A VM adds a hypervisor boundary. Containers separate less deeply.

items.prompt: In the table picture, who is the shared table?
choices: The host's kernel
The image
The registry
items.explanation: Every container sits at the same table, which is the host kernel.

items.prompt: Why can a container image stay small?
choices: A registry zips it into a file
It leaves out the app's own source code
It carries no whole operating system
items.explanation: The image holds the app and its files, not a guest OS.

items.prompt: Which sentence describes a trade-off rather than a flaw?
choices: Containers can only run one at a time
Containers each need their own private kernel
Containers isolate less deeply for speed
items.explanation: A thinner wall is the price paid for starting fast and packing densely.

items.prompt: How many kernels do ten containers on one Linux host use?
choices: Ten, one for each
One, the host's
None, they run without one
items.explanation: Containers share the single host kernel.

items.prompt: A team runs many small services on one host and is moving them from virtual machines to containers. What does it mainly save?
choices: Repeated application code, since containers share a single copy of every service they run
Repeated network ports, since containers share one address and never need separate ones
Repeated guest operating systems, since containers share the host kernel instead of each carrying one
Repeated image builds, since containers are created directly from the running host
items.explanation: The saving is the per-guest operating system. App code and ports are still needed by each service.
items.reference:
Table and chairs
VM: each guest brings its own whole operating system
container: each guest brings only its app and files
shared table = the host's kernel, used by every container
trade: lighter and faster, but a thinner wall between neighbours
Why: containers skip the guest operating system by sharing the host kernel, which buys speed and size at the cost of a thinner wall.
items.learnMore:
Sharing a kernel

A virtual machine boots a complete guest operating system on virtual hardware. A container is an ordinary process on the host, started with its own view of files and processes. That is why it starts quickly and why many fit on one machine, and also why a kernel flaw affects every neighbour.

Common mistake

Thinking a container image contains a kernel. It does not; the container borrows whatever kernel the host is running.
items.reflection: Think of an apartment building compared with separate houses. Which shared parts save money, and which would you rather not share?

items.prompt: A reviewer prefers VMs for running code from unknown customers. Which reasoning fits?
choices: Containers store their files unencrypted, while a VM encrypts every file it holds by default on the host
Containers cannot be given CPU or memory limits, while a VM can always be limited precisely and strictly
Container images are larger than VM images, so they expose more of the host to outsiders
Containers share the host kernel, so one kernel flaw could reach neighbours, while a VM adds a hypervisor boundary
items.explanation: The concern is the shared kernel. Both can be limited, and neither encrypts files by default.

items.prompt: A colleague says a container ships its own kernel, so it behaves the same on any host kernel version. What is wrong with that?
choices: The image holds a kernel, but it is replaced by the registry whenever the image is pulled again
The image has no kernel; the container uses the host's, so its kernel behaviour varies by host
The image holds a kernel, but it only activates when the host has no kernel of its own
The image holds no kernel, so a container cannot make system calls until one is installed
items.explanation: Containers make system calls to the host kernel. They need no kernel of their own, and they inherit the host's kernel features and quirks.

choices: A container skips loading the app's files, while a VM reads every file again from the registry each time
A container is compressed more tightly, while a VM must be unpacked before it starts
A container starts a process on a running kernel, while a VM must boot a whole guest operating system

items.prompt: What does each important Dockerfile instruction add?
choices: A new container
A layer to the image
A second Dockerfile
items.explanation: Most instructions add a filesystem layer. A few only update metadata.

items.prompt: What does Docker do when a layer's inputs have not changed?
choices: Reuses the cached layer
Rebuilds it anyway
Deletes it from the image
items.explanation: A matching cache key means the work can be skipped.

items.prompt: In which direction does a rebuild spread?
choices: Forward, to every later layer
Backward, to every earlier layer
Sideways, to unrelated images
items.explanation: Later layers sit on top of the changed one, so they must rebuild too.

items.prompt: Only server.js changed in a well-ordered Dockerfile. Which layer rebuilds?
choices: The base image layer at the bottom
The dependency install layer above it
The layer that copies the source
items.explanation: Only the source copy depends on server.js.

items.prompt: What should come first in a well-ordered Dockerfile?
choices: Copy all source, then install
Run the app, then install
Copy the manifest, then install
items.explanation: The install then depends only on the manifest files.

items.prompt: Which layer is usually the slowest in a Node build?
choices: Setting the working directory
The dependency install
Copying one small file
items.explanation: Downloading and unpacking packages dominates the build time.

items.prompt: Where do rarely changing steps belong?
choices: Last in the Dockerfile
Early in the Dockerfile
In a separate registry
items.explanation: Early layers stay cached through most changes.

items.prompt: What makes the install layer rerun in a well-ordered Dockerfile?
choices: A change to the manifest or lockfile
Any edit to any source file
Starting the container twice in a row
items.explanation: Only the manifest files feed the install layer's cache key.

items.prompt: A five-layer Dockerfile runs FROM, WORKDIR, manifest copy, install, source copy. Only the manifest changes. Which layers rerun?
choices: The manifest copy, the install, and the source copy
Only the manifest copy, since no other layer reads that file directly
Only the install and source copy, since a file copy is never cached at all
All five, since a changed file always forces a new base image to be pulled
items.explanation: The manifest copy is the first changed layer, so it and everything above it rebuild. FROM and WORKDIR stay cached.
items.reference:
One change, and what reruns
edit server.js only: just the source-copy layer
edit package.json or lockfile: manifest copy, install, source copy
change the base image: every layer after FROM
the cascade only runs forward, never backward
Why: each layer's cache key includes the layer below it, so a change forces everything above it to rebuild.
items.learnMore:
Layer order is a speed decision

Docker reuses a layer when its instruction and inputs match the last build and every layer beneath it was also reused. Put the slow, rarely changing steps first and the fast, often changing ones last, and most rebuilds only touch the top.

Common mistake

Thinking the cache works per file. It works per layer in order: one change lower down throws away everything above it, even layers whose own inputs did not change.
items.reflection: Think of a multi-step recipe or report you rebuild often. Which step is slow and rarely changes, and could you move it earlier?

items.prompt: A Dockerfile copies the whole project, then installs dependencies. A teammate edits only a README and the install reruns. Why?
choices: The README is a manifest file, so editing it always counts as a dependency change
The install sits above a copy of the whole tree, and the README is part of that tree
Docker re-runs every install when any file in the project has a newer timestamp
The install reads the README to find out which packages to fetch from the registry
items.explanation: Docker cannot know the README is irrelevant. It only sees that the copy layer's inputs changed, so the install above it is invalid too.

items.prompt: A native-library install step is being added that depends only on the base image. Where should it go for the best reuse?
choices: Last, after the source copy, so that it always sees the newest version of the whole code base
Between the install and the source copy, so that it follows the app's own packages
Anywhere, because Docker caches each instruction separately from the ones around it
Right after the base image, before the manifest copy, since its inputs rarely change
items.explanation: Stable steps go early so they stay cached through source and manifest edits. Position decides what invalidates them.

items.prompt: The base image tag is bumped by one patch version and nothing else changes. How much of the cache survives?
choices: None; the changed foundation invalidates FROM and so every layer built on it
All but FROM, since the other layers' own inputs are exactly as they were before
Only the install layer, since it is the one that holds the most data to carry over
Only the layers before the manifest copy, since later ones read the application files
items.explanation: A layer is only reusable if everything beneath it is. Changing FROM changes the bottom, so nothing above it can be reused.

items.prompt: What does a multi-stage build separate?
choices: Building the app from running it
Images from the containers they start
Tags from digests in a registry
items.explanation: Build tools live in an early stage, and the runtime stage stays lean.

items.prompt: What ends up in the final image?
choices: Everything from every stage
Only the first stage
Only what the last stage holds
items.explanation: Earlier stages are used for building and then left behind.

items.prompt: Which keyword pulls files from an earlier stage?
choices: RUN --copy
FROM --old
COPY --from
items.explanation: COPY --from names a stage and the path to take from it.

items.prompt: Does a file written in stage one exist in stage two automatically?
choices: Yes, stages share one filesystem
No, it must be copied across
Yes, but only files under 1 MB
items.explanation: Each stage starts clean.

items.prompt: Why leave the compiler out of the final image?
choices: The app runs slower with it
Smaller image and less to attack
Registries refuse images that contain it
items.explanation: Unused tools add size and extra attack surface for no benefit.

items.prompt: What does each FROM line start?
choices: A fresh stage
A new registry
A second container
items.explanation: A FROM begins a new stage on its own base.

items.prompt: Compiled output sits in /app/dist in the build stage. How does the runtime stage get it?
choices: COPY it with --from=build
It arrives on its own
Run the compiler again at runtime
items.explanation: Nothing crosses stages unless it is named.

items.prompt: What happens if the COPY --from line is forgotten?
choices: The build stops with an error
The files appear anyway
The image builds but lacks the files
items.explanation: The build succeeds. The failure only shows when the container runs.

items.prompt: The build stage installs dev dependencies, including a TypeScript compiler. The runtime stage copies only dist/. Is the compiler in the final image?
choices: Yes; every stage's installed packages are merged into the image that gets shipped
Yes; the compiler is added when the output in dist/ was produced by it
No; the final image holds only the runtime stage plus what it explicitly copied
No; but only if the build stage is named exactly build in the Dockerfile
items.explanation: The final image is the last stage. Stage 1's packages never cross unless a COPY --from names them.
items.reference:
Workshop and delivery truck
stage 1 (build): compiler, dev tools, raw source
COPY --from=build: names exactly what crosses over
stage 2 (runtime): fresh start plus only the copied output
the final image is stage 2; stage 1 is left behind
Why: each FROM starts a clean stage, so only what is explicitly copied across reaches production.
items.learnMore:
Multi-stage builds

A single-stage image keeps every tool it ever used. A multi-stage build uses an early stage to compile, then starts over from a clean base and copies in only the finished output. The result is smaller to pull and has fewer things an attacker could use.

Common mistake

Assuming stages share an environment the way consecutive instructions in one stage do. Files, packages and ENV values from one stage do not exist in the next unless copied.
items.reflection: Think of building furniture: sawdust and tools stay in the workshop and only the finished piece goes to the customer. What in your work is workshop and what is delivered?

items.prompt: A build succeeds, but the container crashes at start with a missing dist/server.js. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Stage one failed silently, because a successful build never proves that compiling worked
The registry dropped dist/ while pushing, because it removes folders it considers temporary
The runtime base image deletes any folder called dist when a container starts
Stage two never received dist/, because nothing crosses stages unless COPY --from names it
items.explanation: The build only checks that each instruction ran. Forgetting the cross-stage copy leaves an image that is valid but incomplete.

No; ENV lines are ignored in any Dockerfile that has two stages

items.prompt: Why is the isolation between stages a benefit rather than a limitation?

items.explanation: Isolation makes the default safe: leaving something out is automatic, and including it takes an explicit line.

items.prompt: What is a registry?
choices: A list of running containers
A tool that writes Dockerfiles
A store where built images are kept by name
items.explanation: Registries hold images so other machines can pull them.

items.prompt: Which command uploads an image to a registry?
choices: docker pull
docker push
docker build
items.explanation: push uploads, pull downloads.

items.prompt: Which command downloads an image?
choices: docker push
docker pull
docker run
items.explanation: pull fetches layers the machine does not already have.

items.prompt: What is myapp:1.4.2?
choices: An image name with a version tag
A container's process number
A registry password
items.explanation: The part after the colon is the tag.

items.prompt: In a build-once setup, what does CI do?
choices: Builds and pushes one image
Rebuilds in every environment
Edits the image on each server
items.explanation: One build, many pulls, identical bytes.

items.prompt: Why can a pull download only some layers?
choices: Registries only store some layers
Layers expire after one use
Layers already on the machine are reused
items.explanation: Layers are stored and shared individually.

items.prompt: Which reference is the most exact?
choices: The tag latest
The image's file name
A content digest
items.explanation: The digest comes from the image content itself.

items.prompt: Can the tag latest point to different images over time?
choices: No, it is locked once pushed
Yes, it is just a movable label
Only if the registry is private to one team
items.explanation: Anyone with push rights can move any tag.

items.prompt: Two deploys a week apart both run docker pull myapp:latest. Are they guaranteed to get the same bytes?
choices: No; latest is a movable label, so it may point to a different image by the second deploy
Yes; a tag is locked to the first image pushed under it for as long as the registry exists
Yes; Docker keeps a local copy and always prefers it over anything in the registry
No; but only because the second deploy runs on a different day of the week
items.explanation: A tag is a pointer that can be moved. Only a digest guarantees the exact content.
items.reference:
Tag versus digest
tag (myapp:1.4.2): a label; can be moved to a different image
latest: a label too, with no promise of staying put
digest (@sha256:...): derived from the image's contents
same digest = same bytes, always
Why: a tag names an image and may be repointed, while a digest identifies exact content and cannot be.
items.learnMore:
Registries, tags and digests

A registry stores images by name and tag, and underneath by a content digest. Pushing uploads only layers the registry lacks; pulling downloads only layers the machine lacks. Build once in CI, push once, and every environment pulling that digest gets identical bytes.

Common mistake

Treating a tag as a guarantee. A tag, including latest, is a movable pointer; only a digest pins the exact content.
items.reflection: Think of a book title that gets new editions compared with one specific copy's serial number. Where in your work does a name quietly stop meaning the same thing?

items.prompt: Which reference guarantees identical bytes on every pull?
choices: myapp:1.4.2, since version numbers can never be reused once a registry has them
myapp@sha256:<digest>, since the digest is derived from the image content
myapp:stable, since a tag with a name like that is protected from being moved
myapp:latest-1, since the number at the end is stored with the image layers
items.explanation: Version tags are usually stable by convention, but only the digest is enforced by the content.

items.prompt: CI builds once, and staging, QA and production all pull the same digest. What does that close?
choices: The gap in data, since every environment now reads the same database rows
The gap in traffic, since each environment now receives the same number of requests
The gap in hardware, since the registry rewrites the image to suit each host
The gap from rebuilding, since each environment runs the identical built artifact
items.explanation: Rebuilding in each place risks different base images or package versions. Pulling one artifact removes that risk.

items.prompt: A server already has four of an image's five layers cached. What does docker pull transfer?
choices: Only the one missing layer, since layers are stored and shared individually by content
The whole image again, since a pull always replaces what the machine already has
Only the top layer, since the lower four are always assumed to match the registry
Nothing, since a partly cached image is treated as complete and is never topped up
items.explanation: Layers are identified by content, so a machine only needs the ones it lacks.

items.prompt: Implement `hasChanged(layer, changed)`. `layer` is `{ name, inputs }` and `changed` is an array of input names. Return true if any of the layer's inputs is in `changed`.
items.explanation: A layer is directly affected when at least one of its inputs appears in the changed list.

items.prompt: Implement `firstChangedIndex(layers, changed)`: the index of the first layer (in order) with a changed input, or -1 if none. Each layer is `{ name, inputs }`.
items.explanation: findIndex stops at the first layer with a changed input and returns -1 when there is none. That index is where the cascade starts.

items.prompt: Implement `layersFrom(names, index)`: the layer names from position `index` to the end. If `index` is -1, nothing rebuilds, so return an empty array.
items.explanation: Everything from the first changed layer onward rebuilds. slice(-1) would wrongly return the last element, so -1 needs its own case.

items.prompt: Implement `cachedLayers(names, rebuilt)`: the names that are not in `rebuilt`, keeping their original order.
items.explanation: Filtering keeps the original order and drops every layer that is marked as rebuilt.

items.prompt: Implement `rebuildSeconds(costs, index)`: `costs` is an array of per-layer seconds. Return the total cost from position `index` to the end, or 0 if `index` is -1.
items.explanation: The cost of a build is the cost of the first changed layer plus every layer after it. With no change, nothing runs.

items.prompt: Implement `computeRebuildPlan(layers, changed)`. `layers` is an array of `{ name, inputs }` in Dockerfile order and `changed` is an array of input names that changed. Return the names of the layers that must rebuild: a layer rebuilds if one of its inputs changed or if any earlier layer rebuilds.

tests.expr: expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'base', inputs: ['image'] }, { name: 'manifest', inputs: ['pkg'] }, { name: 'install', inputs: [] }, { name: 'source', inputs: ['src'] }], ['src'])).toEqual(['source'])

expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'base', inputs: ['image'] }, { name: 'manifest', inputs: ['pkg'] }, { name: 'install', inputs: [] }, { name: 'source', inputs: ['src'] }], ['pkg'])).toEqual(['manifest', 'install', 'source'])
expect(computeRebuildPlan([{ name: 'base', inputs: ['image'] }, { name: 'manifest', inputs: ['pkg'] }, { name: 'install', inputs: [] }], ['image'])).toEqual(['base', 'manifest', 'install'])

items.explanation: One forward pass with a flag. The flag turns on at the first layer with a changed input and stays on, so every later layer is included.
items.reference:
The invalidation rule
1. walk the layers from the top of the Dockerfile down
2. a layer reruns if one of its own inputs changed
3. once one layer reruns, every later layer reruns too
never rebuild an earlier layer because of a later edit
Why: the rule is one forward scan with a single flag that turns on at the first change and never turns off.
items.learnMore:
The cache rule as a function

A layer is rebuilt if its inputs changed, or if anything beneath it was rebuilt. That is a single pass with one boolean. Writing it makes the cascade concrete: the output is always a suffix of the layer list, starting at the first changed layer.

Common mistake

Rebuilding only layers whose own inputs changed. That misses the cascade: a layer with no changed input still reruns if a layer beneath it did.
items.reflection: Think of any pipeline where a change early on forces every later step to redo its work. How would you reorder the steps to shrink the redo?

items.prompt: Implement `countCached(layers, changed)`: how many layers can be reused from cache. Layers are `{ name, inputs }` in order; a layer is reused only if neither it nor any earlier layer has a changed input.

tests.expr: expect(countCached([{ name: 'a', inputs: ['i'] }, { name: 'b', inputs: [] }, { name: 'c', inputs: ['s'] }], ['s'])).toBe(2)
expect(countCached([{ name: 'a', inputs: ['i'] }, { name: 'b', inputs: [] }, { name: 'c', inputs: ['s'] }], ['i'])).toBe(0)

items.explanation: Reuse stops at the first changed layer, because everything after it must rebuild. Counting layers before that point gives the cached total.

items.prompt: Implement `buildSeconds(layers, costs, changed)`. `layers` is `{ name, inputs }` in order, `costs` is the seconds each layer takes when it runs (same order), and `changed` lists changed input names. Return the total seconds of the layers that rebuild (a changed layer and every layer after it).

tests.expr: expect(buildSeconds([{ name: 'm', inputs: ['p'] }, { name: 'i', inputs: [] }, { name: 's', inputs: ['src'] }], [1, 20, 2], ['src'])).toBe(2)
expect(buildSeconds([{ name: 'm', inputs: ['p'] }, { name: 'i', inputs: [] }, { name: 's', inputs: ['src'] }], [1, 20, 2], ['p'])).toBe(23)

items.explanation: The same cascade flag decides which layers run, and their costs are added as they are included. A source-only edit costs only the last layer; a manifest edit costs the install too.

items.prompt: What is the build context?
choices: The list of layers in an image
The folder Docker receives to build from
A running container's memory
items.explanation: It is everything in the directory you give to docker build.

items.prompt: What does COPY . . copy into the image?
choices: The whole build context
Only the Dockerfile
Only the last layer
items.explanation: The first dot is the context; the second is the destination.

items.prompt: What does a .dockerignore file do?
choices: Filters files out of the context
Hides the image from the registry
Tells containers to skip their startup
items.explanation: Ignored paths never reach the build.

items.prompt: Which folder usually belongs in a Node project's .dockerignore?
choices: src
package.json
node_modules
items.explanation: The image installs its own packages, so the local ones are noise.

items.prompt: Why ignore .git in the build context?
choices: The app needs it to start up
Docker cannot read folders that start with a dot
It is large and unrelated to the app
items.explanation: It adds weight and changes on every commit.

items.prompt: Which file is .dockerignore most like?
choices: package.json
.gitignore
Dockerfile
items.explanation: Both list path patterns to leave out.

items.prompt: Which file should stay out of an image so secrets do not ship?
choices: server.js
.env
Dockerfile
items.explanation: Environment files often hold passwords and keys.

items.prompt: Without a .dockerignore, what happens to junk files?
choices: They are sent and hashed each build
Docker skips them on its own when it can tell
They are deleted from your disk
items.explanation: Docker has no way to know which files are junk.

items.prompt: A project has a large .git folder and a local node_modules but no .dockerignore. Builds feel slow even for a README edit. Why?
choices: Docker reads the git history to find out which commit to build, and that is slow on large repositories
The node_modules folder is deleted and reinstalled on every build because it is outside the Dockerfile
The whole folder is sent as build context each time, and COPY . . folds all of it into one layer's key
A README edit is treated as a manifest change, which forces the base image to be pulled again
items.explanation: Sending and hashing unrelated files costs time on every build, whatever you edited.
items.reference:
What Docker receives
build context: the whole folder, sent before the Dockerfile runs
COPY . . can reach anything inside that folder
.dockerignore: filters paths out before they are sent
typical entries: node_modules/, .git/, *.log, .env
Why: files filtered out of the context cannot be sent, hashed or copied into a layer.
items.learnMore:
Build context and .dockerignore

Before running any instruction, Docker receives the build context, which is the folder you pointed it at. COPY . . then folds whatever is in that folder into a layer and its cache key. A .dockerignore keeps large, irrelevant or private paths out of that step, using the same glob style as a .gitignore.

Common mistake

Assuming COPY . . only copies what the app needs. It copies everything in the context, including files that change on every commit and files that should never ship.
items.reflection: Think of packing a suitcase from a whole bedroom. What do you need to leave out on purpose so it stays light and private?

items.prompt: .env is added to .dockerignore, and the Dockerfile still has COPY . . Does .env end up in the image?
choices: Yes; COPY . . ignores the filter and takes every file that sits next to the Dockerfile
Yes; .dockerignore only affects docker run, so the build still sees every file
No; but only because the file name starts with a dot and Docker skips those
No; ignored paths are not in the context, so COPY . . cannot reach them
items.explanation: The filter is applied before the build starts, so nothing listed in it can be copied.

choices: Each commit renames the Dockerfile, which forces every layer in the image to be rebuilt
No .dockerignore, so .git changes with each commit and is hashed into the COPY . . layer's key
Git rewrites the dependency manifest on every commit, which invalidates the install layer
The registry marks a layer expired whenever the repository that produced it gets a commit
items.explanation: COPY . . depends on every file in the context, including the changing .git folder.

items.prompt: How does a .dockerignore differ from a .gitignore?
choices: Same job, because ignoring a path in either file removes it from both the image and the repository, too
Different pattern style, because a .dockerignore only accepts exact file names and no globs
Same pattern style, but one filters the build context while the other keeps files out of version control
Same file, because Docker reads the .gitignore directly when no .dockerignore is present
items.explanation: They look alike but act at different points: one before the build, the other when committing.
